final_answer:
Short answer: under the Guidelines it should not matter much which office indicts, provided one office brings a single prosecution that reaches all the false claims; the stronger approach is one consolidated indictment in whichever district can establish venue for both states' claims. Separate prosecutions in each district would not increase the Guidelines time, and would probably lower or equalize it.

1. Venue limits each office. Each execution of a scheme under 1347 is a separate offense, and venue generally lies where the offense was committed. Under 18 U.S.C. 3237(a), an offense begun in one district and completed in another, or committed in more than one district, may be prosecuted in any district in which it was begun, continued, or completed. If the false claims are one continuing scheme that touches both districts (for example, a single billing operation or common payor, with claims processed or paid in one district), a single office could charge the whole scheme. If the Georgia claims and South Carolina claims are truly separate executions with no link to the other district, each office can charge only the counts that occurred in its district. I did not locate case law on the multi-district 1347 venue question, so that factual determination is left unresolved.

2. Guidelines treatment. Section 1347 offenses are sentenced under USSG 2B1.1, a guideline listed in 3D1.2(d), so all counts group and the offense level is driven by aggregate loss. Under 1B1.3(a)(2), conduct that is part of the same course of conduct or common scheme or plan as the offense of conviction counts as relevant conduct even if uncharged or charged elsewhere. Fraudulent claims in both states by the same doctor, same practice, same modus operandi will very likely qualify. Therefore either office's sentencing court can count the other state's losses toward the loss table (and loss-based and health-care-specific enhancements, such as the 2B1.1(b)(7) federal health care offense enhancement for government programs). That reduces the advantage of choosing one office over the other. Fourth and Eleventh Circuit differences about loss (intended vs actual) were largely addressed by the November 2024 Commission amendment moving the loss definition into the guideline text; I did not independently verify this in this run.

3. Why separate prosecutions do not help the government. If the doctor is prosecuted in both districts, the second sentencing court faces USSG 5G1.3(b): when the undischarged term results from offenses fully taken into account as relevant conduct, the new sentence must run concurrently. Only if the other conduct is not relevant conduct does 5G1.3(d) give discretion to run consecutively. So the same relevant conduct is counted once. A single indictment also allows stacking under 5G1.2(d) when the guideline range exceeds the 10-year statutory maximum of one count (1347(a) has a 10-year max per count, 20 years if serious bodily injury, and life if death results), which makes the consolidated approach produce at least as much time as separate cases.

4. Bottom line: the office that can properly establish venue over the entire scheme, ideally the district where the larger share of the scheme, claims, loss, or the doctor's principal operation lies, should obtain one indictment covering both states' claims with many counts. If venue exists in only one district per state, the office that indicts first matters little because loss aggregates as relevant conduct, and the second prosecution would be concurrent, not additional. Caveats: I could not retrieve primary text of the Guidelines Manual or 1347 directly (some sites were blocked), so quotations of guideline text rely on search summaries of Commission materials; and the answer depends on facts about the scheme, payors and amounts not given.

claims.text: Venue for each 1347 execution lies where it occurred; a continuing scheme spanning both districts can be prosecuted in either under 3237(a), permitting one consolidated indictment.
Losses from the other state's claims are likely relevant conduct and aggregate under 2B1.1/3D1.2(d), so the choice of office matters little to the Guidelines range.
Separate prosecutions would produce concurrent sentences to the extent conduct is relevant conduct (5G1.3(b)), so a single consolidated prosecution is best for maximizing time.
